speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak on behalf of the Government to Bill C-65, an Act to amend the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act. Before reporting on the outcome of the hearings on Bill C-65 at committee stage, I would like to take a few moments to remind Members of the House of the essential features of this proposed legislation.
A most important feature of Bill C-65 is the establishment of the RCMP public complaints commission, and procedures for the handling of complaints by the public against RCMP members. The establishment of the public complaints mechanism is a contemporary response to the need for objective and open handling of complaints, which will undoubtedly command public confidence.
A second important feature of the Bill relates to the establishment of procedures to deal with matters internal to the Force, such as grievances of individual members, disciplinary and discharge matters.
The most significant aspect of these proposed procedures relates to the appeal process and, in particular, to the establishment of an external review committee. This review authority will be external to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and independent of it. It will be able to look into certain grievance decisions, formal disciplinary sanctions and discharge or demotion.
In formulating the proposals in these areas, every effort has been made to balance the interests of the members of the public and of the RCMP against the need for continued effectiveness of the Force. There is not a more respected and efficient police force in the world. This legislation will only serve to enhance the operation of the Force.
During the legislative committee hearings on Bill C-65, which lasted for several weeks, the committee had the benefit of hearing from a number of witnesses who represented a


RCMP Act
variety of interests in this legislation. These witnesses are to be complimented for their able presentations which very much assisted the committee. Special attention should be paid to the excellent submissions of the Division staff relations representatives who presented the views and concerns of the majority of the members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to Bill C-65. As a consequence of the witness' submissions, a number of important amendments to the Bill were adopted by the legislative committee. I propose to review these amendments briefly for the House at this time.
The first major change to Bill C-65 relates to representation before the external review committee. The Bill originally provided for representation by counsel only. The appropriate sections have now been amended to allow for representation by either counsel or a representative from within the Force at a hearing before the external review committee. This amendment is significant in that it allows those giving evidence before the committee to save substantial costs by being represented by members as opposed to counsel.
[DOT] (mo)
A second significant amendment to Bill C-65 relates to public complaints with respect to the conduct of a member of the Force. Previously, Bill C-65 provided that the public could complain about any conduct of an RCMP member. The appropriate sections of Bill C-65 have now been amended to restrict the type of conduct which can form the basis of a complaint to a member's conduct in the performance of any duty or function under the Act.
The purpose of this amendment is to ensure that public complaints relate only to conduct with respect to a member's statutory duties and is based upon the rationale that a member of the Force, like any other citizen, has a right to privacy.
Another amendment adopted in respect of the public complaints process relates to the authority of the Public Complaints Commission to investigate a complaint. In addition to these substantive amendments to Bill C-65, there were a variety of amendments adopted by the committee which, while of a more technical nature, will undoubtedly serve to enhance the legislation as a whole. I am positive that upon passage of Bill C-65, the new amended RCMP Act will represent comprehensive, progressive legislation which will benefit both members of the RCMP and the citizens of Canada alike for many years to come.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to remind the House that the passage of this Bill has been subject to several delays in the past such that the proposed amendments to the RCMP Act are now long overdue. Accordingly, I would urge Hon. Members of the House to co-operate in ensuring expeditious passage of this Bill so that the RCMP Act may be amended to bring it into line with modern times and with the current needs of the RCMP and its members.

Mr. Speaker, much discussion was given to this subject in committee and it was my judgment, perhaps, as Parliamentary Secretary during the hearings, that the majority of members did not necessarily want to have collective bargaining. They were satisfied with the methods now used through their divisional representatives.
Further to that, the point did come out that the differential in payment between other police across Canada and the


RCMP was less than $500 on the average. If the members of the Force become members of a union or a collective bargaining unit, there would be a grave possibility that that $500 would be lost in union dues.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Parliamentary Secretary on the same point. Given the fact that all other police forces, municipal and provincial, as far as 1 can tell, belong to organizations which bargain for them with the employer, whether it be the municipality or the province, and given the fact that the bargaining processes deal not just with the question of wages and hours but with grievances, along with everything else, surely the Government would accept the idea that the RCMP, like all other federal Public Service employees, should be permitted to belong to an organization if they so wish? Surely the question of whether it is worth it for them to belong, and whether that $500 would go towards union dues, is a question they should decide as free Canadians rather than having the Government make that decision for them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps the Hon. Member did not hear my earlier comment in answer to a previous question. In our judgment, the majority of the members of the Force are not requesting that kind of legislation at this time. Therefore, being a democratic and open Government, we are not going to push this onto a group of people, especially the people who form the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. That force is not like other police organizations in our country. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police is unique. There is not another Force like it in the country. Certainly we are very conscious of its needs and requests and we react accordingly.

Mr. Speaker, I am puzzled by the answer I received from the Parliamentary Secretary. How does the Department know that a majority of the RCMP officers do not want to belong to a union? If I understand the labour legislation which applies both federally and provincially, when a union or association wants to represent a group of employees, it has to try to sign up the particular group. It has to demonstrate to the Labour Relations Board or, I suppose in this case, it would be the Public Service Staff Relations Board, that it has signed up a majority of the affected people. If there is then any doubt, a vote is called which is supervised by the proper Government agency, and if the majority indicates it wants to belong, it then gets certification.
If, as the Government says, a majority of the RCMP officers do not want to belong, then they could indicate that in a vote and that would be the end of it. But whenever the Government adopts its usual "we know best" paternalistic attitude, which does not apply to any other group of employees except, perhaps, the employees who work on Parliament Hill- and the Government is even proposing to give them the right to collective bargaining-I find it very strange.

Mr. Speaker, I had a number of other questions for my distinguished colleague, the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata), but I will ask them on another occasion.
I am pleased to rise and participate in third reading debate on this important and long overdue legislation. It set out to accomplish two basic objectives. Initially the purpose of the legislation was to establish a system of review external to the RCMP of the complaints made by members of the Force, a grievance procedure of substance as opposed to the rather paternalistic and Neanderthal labour relations policies which are currently governing the RCMP.
The second major area of concern was the question of complaints made by members of the public about activities, either about the Force generally or about individual members. Those are the two basic objectives of the Bill.


The Bill is based very loosely on recommendations of the Marin Commission which was established in 1974. Your Honour will recall that that commission was established following certain allegations made by a number of disgruntled members of the RCMP about the practices and policies of the Force at that time.
Since the commission issued its report in 1976, almost 10 years ago now, there have been a succession of Bills by Liberal Governments and now the Conservative Government on this question.
There is no question that this legislation does represent an improvement over the status quo. We in the New Democratic Party believe it falls far short of legislation which would truly bring into the twentieth century the practices and policies of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, both in the area of Labour relations and in the area of review of public complaints.

The fundamental concern in respect of the external review process remains. It still denies freedom of association to members of the Force. I am confident that that will be struck down by the courts as being in breach of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, just as other provisions of the Act are in breach of the Charter. The final point with regard to the whole question of external review of grievances is that at the end of the day, after the external review committee has met and considered the grievance, it is still the commissioner himself or herself, although that will take a while in the RCMP, I suspect, who has the final word. The commissioner can reject completely the recommendations made by the external review committee. What kind of grievance procedure is that? Even within the civilian security service there is provision for a grievance procedure which would in fact ensure that members are not at the mercy of the commissioner on those grievances. Provisions of the Bill on external review remain seriously flawed.
A second major area of the Bill is the provisions in respect of public complaints, complaints about either policies of the RCMP generally or with regard to an individual member of the Force. Unfortunately the Bill, as was noted by the Hon. Member for York South-Weston, has not accepted the recommendation of the Marin Commission-and in fact the provisions of previous Bills-which ensured that complaints about general policy matters could in fact be brought before the public complaints commission. It is not good enough to suggest, as the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) suggested yesterday, that individual complaints may give rise to policy questions. If a member of the public has a concern about the resources which are deployed by the RCMP in a particular community, if a member of the public has a concern about a policy matter which perhaps a member of the RCMP individually would not wish to raise, he or she should have the right to raise it directly with the public complaints commission.
I was very pleased that the Government accepted my very important and significant amendment in committee which would give the public complaints commission the right to investigate, independent of the RCMP, complaints which it felt warranted an investigation of an independent nature. My amendment was indeed recommended as well by a number of witnesses who made representations to the committee, including the Canadian Civil Liberties Association. I indicate my support for that decision of the Government and my pleasure that the Government moved forward in this important area of independent investigation of complaints.
The Bill falls far short and indeed makes a mockery of the concept of independent review in one fundamental aspect. After the public complaints commission has conducted its review, has perhaps engaged in independent investigation and has come to the conclusion there has been impropriety or wrongdoing, at the end of the day all it can do is go back to the commissioner and say; "Here you are, Mr. Commissioner, here is our recommendation. You do what you like with it. You can accept it or reject it". It is entirely up to the


commissioner. We have internal review of public complaints which flies directly in the face of a fundamental need for external review and a final decision on the part of the public complaints commission itself.
I quoted Clay Ruby on this point in my comments at report stage when I proposed an amendment which would have ensured that the public complaints commission would have had the final say. It is not good enough for a police force to investigate itself and make decisions about what disciplinary action will follow from its own misdeeds. This kind of accountability falls far short of what we in the New Democratic Party believe to be essential.
I would note that the Manitoba Police Commission, under the enlightened administration of that province, brought forward a system which ensures that the final decision on public complaints is indeed in the hands of the Manitoba Police Commission, not in the hands of members of the police. We believe that it is important that there be greater accountability to the contracting provinces and the territories. I note the commitment of the Solicitor General in response to my question in committe that indeed the territories would have representation on this public complaints commission as well.
In looking at the process now, we have to ask ourselves: Given the track record of this commissioner, are we satisfied that he will have the final say on public complaints? I have to say that our answer to that is an unequivocal no, absolutely not. For example, it was this commissioner who, following the revelations of wrongdoings, of illegalities and of breaches of the Criminal Code and other federal statutes, said: "I have examined this", and not only was there no prosecution whatsoever, but not one member of the RCMP was subjected to any form of discipline as a result of those wrongdoings.
Some of them were promoted.

Indeed, as the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Oriikow) points out, some of those who were involved in these illegalities and wrongdoings were promoted. That is the commissioner who is being given the final say on public complaints. It is the same commissioner who has advocated that the RCMP should have the right of access to all Government records. It is the same commissioner, it has been suggested by a very senior and respected member of the RCMP, Superintendent A1 Nowlan, who was well aware in 1977 when he was the commissioner designate that he was misleading the then Solicitor General, the Hon. Francis Fox, in respect of the full scope and nature of wrongdoings. It was not, as Francis Fox told the House in 1977, an isolated incident of wrongdoing. Superintendent A1 Nolan has put his reputation on the line and has said that it is his view as a senior member that indeed the commissioner designate, the current commissioner, was well aware at the time that he was deliberately misleading the Minister. I call upon the Justice Committee to give Superintendent Nowlan an opportunity to appear before that committee and to make these very serious allegations before that forum.
RCMP Act
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are signalling that my time on third reading is coming to an end. I want to reiterate our fundamental concern that while this Bill does represent progress in some respects, it falls short of what should be accorded, both in terms of the basic rights of members of the RCMP, and also in terms of the confidence of Canadians in the public complaints commission.
The Hon. Member for Burnaby stretches things a little too far.
It takes one to know one.

It is obvious that the Hon. Member for Burnaby is using his protection in this House with respect to Superintendent Nowlan. Allegations were made and I would simply call upon the Member for Burnaby to call them allegations. He often speaks of legal principles, about the presumption of innoncence and how one has to protect the innocent in society, yet he referred to Mr. Nowlan's accusations as being reality.
If he is acting responsibly as a parliamentarian and an individual trained in law he should not refer to allegations as fact. I agree that the allegation should have been investigated, but I would simply caution the Member not to use his immunity in order to attack individuals. The Hon. Member has done it before when he accused senior Petro-Canada executives of being CIA spies. He used his parliamentary immunity at committee to do this. He subsequently apologized and we accepted that apology. I would simply ask him to be cautious regarding the use of parliamentary privilege as it affects everyone in this House. When allegations are made they should be referred to as such and not as if they are substantiated facts.
The question I would like to put to the Hon. Member for Burnaby is with respect to his Party's position on Bill C-65. He used phrases such as "seriously flawed, makes a mockery of fundamental review, flies directly in the face, the Bill falls far short oF', yet the New Democratic Party intends to support Bill C-65. If the Bill is seriously flawed, as they claim it is, why do they speak with such rhetoric in their opposition to the Bill, yet intend to support it? I mean you cannot whistle and blow at the same time. You either support it or you don't support it.
We have indicated, as far as the Official Opposition is concerned, that we have concerns with respect to the Bill, but they are not fundamental concerns, and we intend to support it. Being an individual of principle, how can the Hon. Member for Burnaby justify his rhetoric and reconcile it with the intent of his Party to support the Bill? I would like to ask him when he speaks, does he speak for the New Democratic Party? 1 know he often makes it clear that he is not, and that his Members at times wince when he takes particular positions on various subjects, but is he truly speaking for the New Democratic Party?


RCMP Act

Unfortunately, I don't have enough time to respond fully to that little rant by the Hon. Member for York South-Weston. If there is one Member out of the 282 Members in this Parliament, who should not lecture anyone about dragging reputations through the mud it is the Member for York South-Weston.
Hear, hear!

I remember day after day as that Member stood in the House and dragged the reputation of the Premier of New Brunswick through the mud based on allegations, which to this day he has not had the courage or integrity to stand up and defend. Don't let him talk in that hypocritcal and phoney manner about dragging reputations through the mud.
The Hon. Member asks, how it is we support this Bill when it is flawed, both in terms of the grievance procedure and in terms of the public complaints process. He is right, the Hon. Member has said that this Bill is largely repeating a Liberal Bill and that Bill was a seriously flawed Bill. We did what we could in committee to improve this legislation. We did what we could at report stage to improve this legislation.
I note that the Liberal Party, and the representative for the Liberal Party who was so concerned about this Bill and, had grave reservations about a number of elements, but, when push came to shove, how many amendments did members of that Party suggest to the Bill at report stage? Did they suggest three or two? No, that Party which was so concerned about this legislation, collective bargaining, improving the grievance procedure, did not suggest one amendment-nothing. Don't let them stand up and sanctimoniously prattle to Members of the House and the public about improving the Bill when they did nothing whatsoever to try to improve the Bill themselves.
On a point of order.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand).
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, as the Solicitor General who appointed the Marin Commission in 1974, I am pleased to see some of his recommendations implemented in Bill C-65. However, I am extremely disappointed that many of his key recommendations have not been accepted.
In particular, I am disappointed that the very strong recommendations made by the RCMP division representatives in their brief and the Association of 17 Divisions, that there be no suspension unless it be with pay and benefits while a charge against the member in question is pending, were not incorporated into the Bill. The division representatives are duly elected by the men of the RCMP throughout the country. They


have a very strong and widely-based support. They recommended that the Bill be amended so that the suspension would be only with pay and benefits. As I said yesterday, it is my firm belief that to suspend any member of the Force pending a charge without pay and benefits is in contravention of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. In the Charter is entrenched the principle that one is innocent until proven guilty. If one is innocent until proven guilty, then there is no basis for a person who is simply charged with a disciplinary infraction, or whatever, to have his pay and benefits suspended. I do not want to enter into the hot debate which just took place between my colleague and the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson).
Why not?

No, I will not. I would rather concentrate on the Bill.
The Hon. Member for Burnaby knows, since we were on the legislative committee together, that we presented a good number of amendments to the Bill in committee.
What about in the House?

As the Hon. Member knows, both his amendments and mine were defeated in committee by the overwhelming Conservative majority. One can only bang one's head up against a wall so many times. Perhaps the Hon. Member for Burnaby has a harder head than I.
No question about that!

Rather than continually formulating amendments which will be voted down without any real consideration by this large Conservative majority, I have better ways to spend my time. It is too bad that those amendments were defeated.
On this particular amendment, there was wide-spread and deep support among the members of the Force. They made that clear before the committee. It was something which was also recommended by the Marin Commission, which spent a good deal of time consulting and studying the issue, not only in Canada with other police forces but outside the country as well.
The other matter the Bill does not deal with, and which I think is unfortunate, is leaving the final decision on public complaints with the Commissioner rather than with an independent authority. That is contrary to all the principles of justice and equity. If one is responsible for the administration of a body, in this case the RCMP, then it is not proper that that person should be the final judge on accusations or complaints made by the public against members of the Force while administering the Force at the same time. That person then becomes both judge and administrator. To me that is not proper. It is unfortunate that the Government has not seen fit to accept an amendment along these lines.
I am pleased to recall that during my term as Solicitor General certain improvements were made to the personnel policy with respect to the RCMP. At that time we brought in,
RCMP Act
for the first time, overtime pay for members of the Force, changes with respect to the marriage rules and the admittance of women into the Force, and the division representative system was set up. The division representative system was certainly a movement in the right direction. According to some members of the Force it is working well.
However, there is still a difficulty in that the RCMP in many of our large cities must work side-by-side with other police forces on joint efforts. The members of those other police forces have the right to collective bargaining. Collective bargaining has been tried in our police forces in the country for several years. It has not been abused.
At the time of the introduction of the division representative system there was not that much experience with collective bargaining. That was in the mid 1970s. I want to make it clear that I am talking about the right to collective bargaining and not the right to strike. The Association of 17 Divisions has not asked for the right to strike. The other police forces in Canada have the right to collective bargaining and they do not have the right to strike. So we are not debating the right to strike issue. However, after this number of years, having seen what has taken place with other police forces in the country, and in light of the fact that the RCMP must work shoulder-to-shoul-der in many cases on drug and organized crime matters with provincial and municipal police forces which have the right to collective bargaining, I believe the time has come for the RCMP to have the right to collective bargaining.
The Hon. Member for Burnaby is right when he says that the Liberal Party did not always take that position. As 1 have said, we have observed what has happened over the years. By the way, we in the Liberal Party are much more broadly based than those in the NDP. We have a much wider range of opinions. We have people in our Party who always believed in the right to collective bargaining and others who did not.
So that cancels it out and makes it neutral, then.

Mr. Speaker, 1 get a great kick out of members of the New Democratic Party. It was an NDP Government in Saskatchewan which came to Ottawa to knock out the entrenchment of women's rights in the Constitution, among other Governments. It was the Blakeney Government with others which did that.
It was the New Democratic Party which got them in.

Their record is far from unblemished when they have been in power. I had to deal with NDP Governments in Manitoba and in British Columbia with respect to Indian rights matters. Their record was far from clean. However, I do not want to get into this matter. I am being provoked by the group over to my left.

Tell us about the neutral Liberals.


RCMP Act

Apart from that, I do not think they are a bad bunch. However, I would like to continue.
Having observed in the country the experience with collective bargaining by other police forces at the municipal and provincial level, I can see no reason whatsoever for continuing to deny this right to members of the RCMP. Even if we are late in coming to the decision, our decision is still valid today. I hope that when we are in Government, in a few years' time, and introduce a Bill on this subject we will have the support of the NDP and even of the Conservatives.
As I have said, there is some improvement in the Bill. However, there is still much to be done. I referred to some of the matters on which work was still required. It is my hope that the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs- and I see that the Chairman of that committee is in the House-will continue to survey the operations of the RCMP in order that we can be made aware of how these changes are being implemented at the administrative level. Perhaps we could be made aware whether or not they are working and how we can continue to make changes so that members of the Force, and members of the public who have complaints against the Force, be justly treated.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there questions or comments? The Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson).

I have just a brief question to ask the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), the former Solicitor General. I believe the Hon. Member was Solicitor General at the time the divisional representative system was established in 1974. He will recall that at that time a vote was taken amongst all the members of the RCMP as to whether or not they wanted to have a division representative system established. At the time the vote was taken, 14 specific promises were made to members with respect to the division representative system. Promise number nine, one of the most important promises, was that: "One divisional representative shall be directly involved in pay negotiation at the bargaining table". Eleven years later, that promise remains unfulfilled.
Would the Hon. Member tell us why he, as Solicitor General, when he had the opportunity to keep that promise, refused to do so? Why is it that members of the RCMP are today still waiting for that promise he made on behalf of his Government in 1974 to be kept?

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the Hon. Member.
I am extremely disappointed that that commitment was not kept. The divisional representative system was started around 1974-1975, and that was one of the commitments which was made. I was Solicitor General at the time, not President of the Treasury Board, and perhaps some day the Hon. Member will have an opportunity to know how things work within Cabinet.
Not unless he becomes a Conservative.

There is push-and-pull, bargaining and lobbying. I cannot reveal what happens in Cabinet, but I myself have raised that question over the years following my tenure as Solicitor General, both as a backbencher on the government side and in hearings in committee on this particular Bill. I asked why representatives of the division were not present at the Treasury Board hearings on this issue. I think the Hon. Member is completely right. 1 support that principle and we have to continue to work within our Party, within Parliament and in the Treasury Board to get it accepted.

Mr. Speaker, in participating in this debate, I would like to say that had the RCMP still had the responsibility for the security service, which it had for so many years, this debate would have been much lengthier, and we would have been much more critical because, along with many other Canadians, I have always had very grave reservations about the activities of the RCMP, particularly with respect to the secrecy upon which it insisted. I am still not satisfied with the secrecy insisted upon by the present service, having to do with matters which occurred 50 and 60 years ago, but this is not the time to debate that.
This Bill is based, somewhat loosely, on the recommendations of the Marin Commission. Justice Marin was appointed by the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) when he was the Solicitor General because of many complaints which were received. The Marin Commission was established in 1976 to study proposals for creating a public complaints bureau in the RCMP and to introduce a formal grievance procedure for members of the Force.
Since the commission issued its report almost 10 years ago, successive Liberal and Conservative Solicitors General have introduced legislation into the House. While the particular version presented by the current Solicitor General does represent an improvement on the status quo, as indicated by the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), there still remains a number of outstanding issues which we have addressed throughout the committee process, and in the House, some of which I would like to put on the record.
These issues focus on two broad areas; First, the degree to which the public complaints commission has any substantive independence and, second, with respect to the grievance procedure. We have questioned its integrity on the basis that the Bill will vest Final decision-making authority on disciplinary action with the commissioner of the RCMP as opposed to giving the final authority to the grievance committee.
In the course of the committee hearings, presentations were made by the Association of 17 Divisions, an organization representing almost 3,000 members of the Force. Its presentation was particularly instructive on the flaws inherent in the Bill's grievance procedure.
Similarly, the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, and its chief spokesperson, Alan Borovoy, raised key concerns with regard to the problems in the Government's proposal for a public complaints commission as outlined in the present Bill.


The major shortcoming in the Government's proposal for the public complaints commission, with which it has refused to deal, is the final decision-making power with respect to any complaint from the public resides with the commissioner of the RCMP. Section 45.46(2) makes this clear. This overriding authority granted to the commissioner is a departure from the spirit and letter of the Marin report. Justice Marin was unequivocal about this aspect of the process. Fie stated, and I quote:
The principal requirement of any credible reviewing authority is that it enjoy the confidence of both the public on whose behalf it is acting and the Force whose actions it is reviewing. Such confidence is possible, in our opinion, if this authority is visibly independent from the RCMP and responsible directly to Parliament rather than to the Government of the Day ... The need for a visibly independent body is based on perceptions held by many who have difficulty in understanding how the Force can be both supervisor and final abiter for public complaints.
That power given to the RCMP, particularly the commissioner, is, as far as I can tell, not given to any other person or body in this country. Regrettably, Bill C-65 rejects the arguments put forward by Mr. Justice Marin. Witnesses who appeared before the Legislative Committee pointed out that the commissioner's ultimately determinant role in the complainants' process may well deter the general public from reporting abuses or complaints, in the knowledge that there will be no outside investigation with substantive decision-making powers about appropriate follow-up action.
In this context, Alan Borovoy of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association stressed the need for an independent investigative role for the public complaints commission. He argued that only independent investigations would ensure that a thorough and partial investigation of complaints is made and, equally important, that such investigations are perceived as independent and impartial. To this end, the Hon. Member for Burnaby proposed an important amendment which would empower the public complaints commission to conduct investigations of complaints where it deemed appropriate. The commission could then use its own staff to investigate a complaint with the power to subpoena witnesses and documents.
Clearly, this amendment, making explicit the investigative powers of the public complaints commission, would have been an important addition to the Bill. However, the broader problem of the final authority of the RCMP commissioner remains. An amendment to deal with this issue was defeated by the Conservatives in committee.
To improve the complaints process, we have also argued that the Bill should impose a reasonable time limit in dealing with public complaints, or at least ensure that a comprehensive status report is sent to the complainant. Members of the public who have made the effort to file a complaint should be kept informed of the progress of their file.
Another important concern is that the Bill does not permit the public to make complaints with respect to general policy concerns about the RCMP, as well as about specific conduct arising out of isolated incidents. I do not want to repeat the arguments I made yesterday, but I remind Members that 1 gave illustrations of the relationship between the RCMP and
RCMP Act
native people on reserves, the role of the RCMP in entrapment in drug cases, and several others.
As addressed in one of our amendments, the issue here is to facilitate the investigation of complaints, such as the hiring policy of the RCMP, or the nature of police services provided, for example, in remote communities. Let me point out there are virtually no members of visible minorities in Canada who are members of the RCMP. There are few, if any, members of the RCMP who are of native origin. That is amazing given the important policing functions the RCMP has regarding native people. I am happy to see the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crosbie) agreeing with me.
Both of these very legitimate issues require that the definition of a complaint be broadened in a way which would permit more policy-oriented issues to be raised by the public and investigated by the commission. The Marin Report anticipated such concerns would fall within the mandate of the commission. In sum, our basic concerns about the public complaints commission are threefold: That the final say on complaints reside with the commission, not the RCMP commissioner; that the RCMP be required to issue a status report to the complainant and, in any event, a time limit be imposed on the investigation; that the definition of a complaint be broadened to allow for policy or administrative concerns to be investigated by the commission.
Regarding the grievance procedure, we believe the second major part of the Bill deals with the establishment of a formal grievance procedure for members of the Force. Fundamentally, the main thrust of our criticisms of this section of the Bill echo the concerns of the Association of 17 Divisions. Their spokesperson came before the committee and argued forcefully that it is time, indeed past time, that members of the Force were entitled to collective bargaining with independent, binding arbitration of grievances, including dismissal, suspension or financial penalties. Such arbitration would be handled by the Public Service Staff Relations Board, similar to the provisions for the Civilian Security Intelligence Service. Why should the Government deny to members of the RCMP what it has given to members of the CSIS by way of labour protection?
The Government refuses to listen to these eminently sensible proposals which would bring labour practices in the RCMP in line with all other major police forces in North America. While I am not a lawyer, I am certain that if RCMP officers take this case to court, given the Charter section which guarantees freedom of association, the Government will be ordered to permit RCMP officers to form an association if they so desire. That simply means the Government will have to pay a substantial amount of money to lawyers to defend the indefensible position it is taking. For a Government concerned about the deficit, that seems to me to be a pretty stupid path to follow.
In light of the Government's unwillingness to move in this important area, we proposed a number of less sweeping measures designed to tighten protection for members of the Force.


RCMP Act
We find unacceptable the provisions which allow for suspension of members without pay and benefits. As it stands now, the Bill flies in the face of the fundamental principle of presumption of innocence. That principle has always been part of our system of justice, we believe, and it is certainly part of our Constitution.
A member of the Force could be suspended by the RCMP commissioner for a year or more, and then be found innocent of the alleged offence or wrong-doing. In the meantime, this person, suspended without pay, may have been forced to sell his or her house, find another job, and certainly not be in a position to bear the costs of legal counsel to ensure adequate representation. In fact, the Association of 17 Divisions cited the example of a member of the Force who, for more than two years, was forced to live on unemployment insurance and savings to support his family. As it turned out, all charges were dropped. Yet great hardship was forced upon the member and his family. We fully support the Association's argument that there should be guarantees written into this Bill to ensure that such unfair situations cannot arise again in the future.
Similar to the major flaw in the public complaints process, the grievance procedure grants the final word on grievances and appeals to the RCMP commissioner. The final say on serious grievances should be with the external review committee, assuming that collective bargaining under the Public Service Staff Relations Act is not accepted or ordered by the courts.
In this context, the Association of 17 Divisions has made three basic points which the Solicitor General has unfortunately chosen to ignore. The first is that the commissioner not constitute the final level of appeal in the grievance process. Secondly, that there be provisions enabling a member to appeal the commissioner's decision to an independent arbitrator. Thirdly, that the RCMP Act be brought in line with the Canada Labour Code and the usual labour practices concerning the submission and adjudication of grievances.
In addition to this fundamental point, we argue that there should be a time limit on the rendering of decisions with respect to grievances. This would guard against excessive delays on the part of the commissioner which cause considerable inconvenience and possibly financial hardship to members concerned. With the right to collective bargaining denied, we proposed an amendment, rejected by the Government, which would permit group grievances to be launched by members of the Force. This provision would allow individual members to speak on behalf of a number of fellow officers in situations where a particular policy or administrative regulation has a similar impact on an entire detachment.
In conclusion, we accept that Bill C-65 is an improvement on the status quo. It codifies rules for grievances and public complaints. However, throughout the committee process the NDP argued that significant amendments are necessary to strengthen this legislation to ensure that the grievance and public complaints process command the respect of members of the Force and the general public. It simply is not acceptable for Parliament to send out the message, in the words of one
expert, that it is proper, fair or just for a police force to investigate itself and make decisions about what disciplinary action to follow from its own misdeeds. Clayton Ruby said that in reference to an earlier version of this Bill. Neither is it acceptable to deny, as this Bill does, the right to collective bargaining for members of the Force. We in the NDP take issue with the Government's in-house approach to grievance adjudication and public complaints investigation. We made clear our support for those groups and individual Canadians who believe that there should be substantive independence for the public complaints committee, and that there should be full collective bargaining for members of the RCMP.
As my colleagues indicated, despite the fact this Bill is an improvement over the status quo, we believe it is still fatally flawed in many respects and we do not propose to support it.
Questions or comments?

Mr. Speaker, after that excellent speech I would like to ask the Hon. Member to elaborate on some concerns he raised in his remarks regarding the Canadian Civil Liberties Association and the role of the commissioner in having the final say. As well, the Hon. Member may wish to elaborate on the comments he made with regard to the language question. He raised some concerns yesterday, and anyone who did not pick up on them yesterday may be watching today. I am concerned, in particular, about the element of leaving the final say with the commissioner. Perhaps the Hon. Member could comment on that.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that if the final say is left to the commissioner, as it is in this Bill, the RCMP, and particularly the commissioner, becomes the complainant, prosecutor, and judge. It seems to me that no individual should have that kind of power. We have a division of authority for everyone else. I have respect for the RCMP and considerable respect for the present Commissioner in particular, however, I do not think that even he should have that kind of power.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is not a major amendment, although it is important to the people affected. The amendment seeks to exempt blind people with seeing-eye dogs from paying the tax on dog food. In terms of revenue gathering, I am sure that it is a very insignificant amount in relation to the several billions of dollars that Bill C-80 will raise for the Government. Exempting blind people from having to pay the tax on dog food is a humane gesture with which, I think, most Members of the House would agree. Government Members who spoke on this in committee generally agreed that blind people should in fact be exempted.
Excise Tax Act
It was pointed out to me after the committee meeting by one of the officials of the Department of Finance that blind people are able to deduct dog food from their income tax. I wonder how many blind people do pay income tax. I suggest that most blind people are poor and that they do not pay much income tax. Therefore, an income tax deduction is not very meaningful to them.
Another area which we would like to have exempted from the tax is feed for horses. Many horses in the country are still used for productive purposes. Horses are still used in the lumbering industry. Religious groups such as the Mennonites and Hutterites still use horses. We are of the opinion that putting a tax on food for horses is wrong.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we are hoping that the Government will accept our amendment in the name of humanity as well as common sense to show that, while it is interested in gathering revenues, it will stop taxing food for guide dogs and for horses used for productive processes. I hope the Government Members will find this amendment acceptable.

Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to speak briefly on Motion No. 19 moved by the Hon. Member from the New Democratic Party which refers to tax on food for guide dogs, and for horses which are used in productive purposes such as farming and logging. 1 certainly support that motion because we still use horses in the logging industry in my province. They are also used for other purposes. In the fishing industry we use horses for raking Irish moss. This is an excellent motion which I hope Government Members will support. It was obviously an oversight in the original legislation. The Government should in no way be taxing food for guide dogs used by blind people because those dogs are a very necessary part of the lives of those people.
I think I could even go a little further and refer to ordinary pets. An awful lot of older people spend a great amount of time with their pets. Many older people do not have families close by and, to some degree, their pet becomes very much a part of their family. I do not think we should put any extra burden on people who are finding it very difficult to get along. I certainly would support this motion.

subsubtopic: EXPORTATION OF FOSSILS TO HARVARD UNIVERSITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Party has long been considered a party of dinosaurs so I am sure that Tory Members will feel a certain kinship with the latest Tory scandal that I have unearthed.
We all know that the Progressive Conservatives have skeletons in their closets going back many, many years. This latest scandal sets a new record for Tory scandals in that it was 200 million years in the making. That is even older than the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen).
The scandal I am referring to is "fossilgate". Last week an announcement was made of a major find of rare fossils near Parrsboro, Nova Scotia. Following this important find, three tons of fossil specimens were illegally shipped to Harvard University in Boston, contrary to the Cultural Property Export and Import Act.
In all the excitement surrounding the discovery, no permit was applied for or granted. I sincerely hope that no harm will come to Canadian heritage in this case and that these fossils will be returned to Nova Scotia after they have been processed and studied.
I ask the Government be more vigilant about making sure that those who need to be aware of the Cultural Property Export and Import Act are made aware of it. We must do everything possible to encourage scientific discovery in Canada, but we must also ensure that our national heritage is protected.

Mr. Speaker, the provision of education to the people of Canada should not be a privilege for those who can afford it, or those fortunate enough to reside in an area of Canada where the population is concentrated. It must be considered a right of all Canadians to be able to receive the education we all need in this ever changing world.
At a recent conference of school committee chairmen looking into special education for native communities, the chiefs raised some very alarming concerns. Among the 19 schools in one part of the Nishnawbe-Aski area of northern Ontario, there is only one gymnasium, one home economics space, and one library. There is not a single science or laboratory facility.
The chiefs also pointed out that during this current school year, the communities of Lac Seul, Sachigo, and Kasibonika had to delay their school openings by at least a month due to repairs. In the community of Wapekeka it has been five years
since the school burned down in 1981. No new school has yet been built. The children have missed classes and have been educated in temporary facilities.
Furthermore, it appears that there is no official policy on native language education in Ontario.
The education of native children is both a treaty right and a moral responsibility of this House and the country. The Government must act immediately to upgrade standards to meet these pressing needs.

subtopic: FORMER INDIAN CONSULATE EMPLOYEE'S APPLICATION FOR REFUGEE STATUS
FORMER INDIAN CONSULATE EMPLOYEE'S APPLICATION FOR REFUGEE STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in mid-January of this year an official of the Indian Consulate-General in Toronto, Mr. Inderjit Singh Bindra, set out to obtain refugee status in Canada. Mr. Bindra decided to give up his diplomatic standing and, in effect, defect to Canada rather than follow the orders of his superiors which were to infiltrate a Sikh temple in Toronto and to organize events which would discredit the Sikh community in Canada.
A spokesman of the India High Commission in Ottawa discredited Mr. Bindra by saying that this was only a ploy by him so that his family could settle in Canada.
The Government of India is highly suspect in this case. One only has to recall the violence of June, 1984, when Indian troops descended upon the Sikh religions holiest shrine, Amritsar's Golden Temple, in a bloody assault upon the Sikh minority, a minority that is struggling for an autonomous homeland.
Mr. Bindra, a Sikh, and his family believe that their lives are in grave danger. That is why they do not wish to return to India. The Bindra family are legitimate refugees in the truest sense and I call upon the Government to do everything in its power to help them remain here, free of the grievous harm that will surely befall them if they are forced to return to India.

Mr. Speaker, the Government must respond by February 25 to the report of the parliamentary committee on equality rights which held hearings from Cape Spear, Newfoundland, to Vancouver, British Columbia. We have heard rumours that the Government is having difficulties in obtaining consensus from its caucus on the 85 recommendations that were unanimously agreed to by the all-party parliamentary committee.
As I have said before, and as others on the committee have said, the recommendations of this committee should not be buffeted about by the prevailing political wind. Issues of personal freedom are simply too sacred and too important to be ignored on a partisan basis.
Discrimination based on sexual orientation must be eliminated. Women should be able, if they wish, to participate alongside men in the Canadian Armed Forces in the interests of their country. Adequate, accessible, and affordable child care services must be available, where desired, by all Canadian parents.
We should not have to fight to achieve equality for all in 1986. It seems from my vantage point, Mr. Speaker, that the enemies of equality will smile and smile, and study you to death. Sometimes we are called upon to speak out for principles, even if they are not politically popular.
Canadians hope to hear the Government say that it is prepared to fight for our Charter of Rights to make it a real bastion of equality, humanity, and decency for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the Bank of Montreal has just published a report on the situation of the building industry in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, this report shows that there will be more growth in the housing sector in Quebec than anywhere else in Canada in the coming months.
You may recall, Mr. Speaker, that not so long ago, so-called experts, of which a number are now warming the benches opposite, forecast a decrease in activity in this sector. As usual, they were wrong. We have witnessed just the opposite, a substantial increase, since housing starts have gone up from 42,000 units in 1984 to 48,000 in 1985.
According to this report, the outlook and the recovery in this sector had not been this favourable for many years. For instance, housing starts have more than doubled since 1982.
Mr. Speaker, these figures and many others just as favourable confirm the fact that Quebecers, like all Canadians, have regained their confidence in the future.
Our colleagues opposite would be well advised to recognize the many achievements of the Government in all fields of activity instead of sinking to partisan politics as the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (M. Malepart) enjoys doing.

subtopic: SUPPORT FOR EXCHANGE VALUE OF DOLLAR-INTERVENTION BY MINISTER OF FINANCE
SUPPORT FOR EXCHANGE VALUE OF DOLLAR-INTERVENTION BY MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to call the attention of the House to the courage shown by Mr. Wilson, our Minister of Finance, in allowing the Bank of Canada to make a significant intervention in support of the Canadian dollar, a move which the Liberals had never done. Indeed, $2.5 billion have been made available to that end.
Private and public sector corporations will benefit with major decrease in the cost of their long-term borrowings of foreign funds.
That intervention was also needed to improve the viability of our bilateral trade talks with the United States.
Let us keep in mind, Mr. Speaker, that the drop in the value of the dollar was engineered by the Liberals. Because of their socialist programs, they caused a drop in our national productivity and hence a reduction in our exports.
The deficit accumulated by the Liberals has discouraged our business people.
The action taken by the Minister of Finance will put an end to that erosion of the value of the Canadian dollar, and put a stop to the short selling of Canadian dollars by speculators of a rather liberal character.

Last week, Mr. Speaker, I accompanied my leader in a tour of the Saguenay region, and we visited the ridings of Chicoutimi, Jonquiere, Lac-Saint-Jean, Roberval, Quebec and Levis.
Mr. Speaker, I have to tell you and the House that the residents of the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean region are wondering whether they are represented here in Ottawa. Somebody in the riding of Chicoutimi even asked me whether the Member is a man or a woman. I have no idea, I have never seen that Member in Ottawa.
Mr. Speaker, we met with the employees of the Desbiens plant and I can say that those people will be here next week
despite the fact that the Hon. Member for Roberval (Mr. Bouchard) threatened them in an attempt to prevent them from asking Liberal or NDP Members to defend their rights. I commend these people who had the courage to call me. They will be here next week to meet with the Members from the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean region and try to find a way to re-open that plant.

Mr. Speaker, February 10 marks the day that wheelchair athlete Rick Hanson completes the half-way point of his "man-in-motion-''world tour. On that day he will arrive in Melbourne, Australia, having travelled exactly one-half the circumference of the globe. He will finish his monumental journey in the spring of 1987 in Vancouver, the city where it all began in March, 1985. He will have visited 33 countries, and will hopefully have reached his goal of raising $10 million for spinal cord research. The funds raised so far remain in the countries he passes through to benefit the disabled living there.
Perhaps even more important, he will have raised the consciousness of the entire world to the plight of the disabled who are denied access to many of the privileges of everyday life because of their disability. In the process he is providing an example of hope for many, many thousands whose lives he touches.
In the coming months he will visit China, Korea, and Japan, and in the fall of this year he will start the final leg of his journey in Newfoundland. His 4,000-mile trek from coast to coast may well be his greatest challenge as he faces the severe weather of a Canadian winter. In all it is estimated that his wheels will have made a total of six million revolutions when his journey is completed.
I ask all Members of the House, all Hon. Senators and all Canadians to make his odyssey a worth-while experience. 1 call upon all Canadians to acknowledge him as a true hero and to support his cause with all the generosity which can be found in our hearts.

Mr. Speaker, on January I the provision which remitted tax on certain allowances and benefits paid to persons residing in the North and in other isolated communities such as Wabush in Labrador was removed. There is little or no positive economic change in northern communities, and the arguments previously put forward are still valid for retaining the remission order. The


economy in northern Canada is reeling from the downturn in Canada's resource industries. The northern tax allowances should immediately be reinstated to help these mostly single industry communities cope with this economic downturn.
I would urge that the Government reinstate the remission provision and consult with northern communities such as Wabush the manner in which the present system can be improved. The Government promised to consult constantly with Canadians. It should immediately honour this commitment by meeting with representatives of northern communities to sort out this problem.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. The Minister has bought massive amounts of Canadian dollars. He has intervened to the extent of $2.4 billion in borrowing in U.S. funds. He knows that he can buy dollars, but he also knows that he cannot buy confidence. A line of credit is no substitute for some coherent fiscal and monetary policy. Would the Minister today tell us the date when he will bring in his Budget, or at least assure us that it will be brought in before the end of February?

Mr. Speaker, the simple answer to the Hon. Member's question is it will be brought in before the end of February. I think the comments that he was making about the coherence of the policy of the Government are totally unfounded. The policy that we have been following to deal with the fiscal problem that we were faced with when we took office a year and a half ago has been regarded as being responsible and absolutely necessary. As I have indicated before in the House, this will continue.
As far as monetary policy is concerned, again we have demonstrated that the monetary policy is designed to lead to non-inflationary growth, and that is exactly what we have had over this past year. Inflation is stable at 4 per cent, and Canada has had the best growth of any of the western industrialized countries, creating 450,000 jobs. That, Mr. Speaker, is sound policy.

Mr. Speaker, indeed inflation has been steadied, thanks to the initiatives of the preceding Government. If everything is as rosy as the Minister pretends perhaps he can tell us why the

bank rate has again increased. We have had an increase today of two-thirds of a per cent. Would he also confirm to the House that the borrowings that he is engaged in in order to protect the dollar will involve additional costs to Canadian taxpayers in present dollar calculations of close to $1 billion?

I don't think the Hon. Member should use that type of alarmist figures without having access to the source of those figures. That will come at the time the Budget is brought down. In response to the increase in the bank rate today, that is a valid question. 1 will be addressing that point in a statement that I propose to make at the end of Question Period today. I would just like to assure him at this point that the combination of our actions in the exchange market, and the interest rate market, are an important combination in dealing with speculative activity which we felt was unnecessary and certainly inappropriate to the economic circumstances that we are in at present.

REQUEST THAT INTEREST RATES BE ROLLED BACK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on my last supplementary might I just say that the Minister has had the courtesy of delivering that statement to me, which I appreciate, but does the Minister agree-as he must, in fact-that each 1 per cent increase in the interest rate-we have had a two-third per cent increase today-costs the average Canadian family renewing a mortgage approximately $600 per year. That is $50 per month. In view of that why doesn't he roll back the interest rates which were jacked up to protect the dollar, as part of the very expensive initiatives which he has taken in his exchange transactions?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT INTEREST RATES BE ROLLED BACK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it is important again to repeat myself. This has to be seen as a package of initiatives designed to meet a specific circumstance. I will be commenting on those initiatives later on today. The initiatives that we have taken over the past couple of days are designed to bring back a degree or normality to the economic situation in this country. That degree of normality had been knocked off track by the speculative pressures in the market-place, which we felt important to meet head-on. That is what we have done.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The Government claims that the dollar crisis is temporary.
Thirty thousand Canadian families will be renegotiating their mortgage this month.
Why would the Government want to punish those families by raising interest rates again today?

Mr. Speaker, as 1 indicated in my response to the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount, what we are trying to do is re-establish some stability in the market-place. That required the combination of actions which we took in the last couple of days. The purpose of doing this is to provide all Canadians with a much more favourable outlook and with better opportunities to deal with the particular personal needs to which the Hon. Member refers. That is our objective. We are confident that that will be the outcome of the actions which we have taken.

Mr. Speaker, I would just remind the Hon. Member that mortgage rates in Canada are still a good deal below the levels they were at the time we took office in September of 1984. So we have made a good deal of progress in spite of the recent uptake we've seen in rates in the last few days.
The increase in rates is much more so in the very short end of the market-place and not much at all in the five-year end.

Mr. Speaker, considering that there are 30,000 families renewing their mortgages this month, and considering that the average increase as a result of what happened today is likely to be $12,000 over the


course of the life of a mortgage, is the Minister of Finance saying to these families that they have to pay the burden of the Government's problems with the dollar?
Mr. Speaker, it is not this Government's problem with the dollar, it's this country's problem we are dealing with here.
Hear, hear!
Who's in charge?
It's the country's fault now.

I am not going to repeat the comments I have made in Question Period in response to the Hon. Member's questions and questions put by the Liberals on the directions of our policies, except to say that what we are doing here is approaching the broad problems the country was facing when we came into office, with a broad range of policy response, including the responses we have seen in recent weeks, and also in areas relating to foreign investment, domestic investment, job creation through programs brought down by my colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, and policies to get the deficit under control to take pressure off the exchange markets and the interest rate markets. This is a broad policy response which, I remind my colleague, has been pretty well received by organizations such as the OECD.
