speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 47(2), I have the honour to table copies in both official languages of the proposed amendments to the Standing Orders.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian economy is performing better than most other industrialized countries' economies. And yet, in face of this, the Canadian dollar has come under sharp downward pressure in recent weeks. The market observers have given a variety of explanations for this weakness. I would like today to put this matter in some perspective and report to the House on the Government's response.
The weakness of commodity prices in general and recent declines in the international price of crude petroleum do have negative implications for our export earnings, but these must be put in perspective.
Canada's net earnings from international trade in petroleum in 1985 were about $2 billion, or less than 2 per cent of our total merchandise exports. The recent fall in oil prices will thus not have a dramatic effect on our trade balance. Even allowing for consequent movements in the prices of our other energy exports does not paint a picture of a sharply deteriorating balance of payments. The existing levels of commodity prices will not have a sufficiently large impact on our resource exports to justify the recent pressure on the exchange rate.
Hon. Members should understand, despite the prevailing caricature, that the strength of Canada's exports extends far beyond the resources sector. Raw materials constituted only 16 per cent of Canada's merchandise exports in 1985. We are now a major exporter of semi-processed and Finished manufactures, and these are an ongoing source of strength for our balance of payments. That strength is assured by Canada's


Statements by Ministers
vastly improved performance in getting our inflation rate down.
Our inflation rate has been about 4 per cent for the past 19 months. Domestic prices and costs have behaved well. Our productivity performance is impressive. This should continue to ensure the competitiveness of Canadian products on world markets. Canada's economy is strong. The growth of our Gross National Product outpaced that of the United States by more than two percentage points last year. That is almost double the rate of growth in the United States. We expect Canada to do better again this year. As a result, the current account of our international balance of payments turned into a small deficit in 1985, and most analysts expect that this small deficit will continue through the course of this year. Apart from the low levels in commodity prices already noted, this is a normal cyclical response to a recovery and reflects the fact that Canada's economy has been growing more quickly than those of most of our major trading partners. A part of that better performance is the stronger growth in business investment expenditures which have a high import content. This shift is contributing to the current account deficit. However, that deficit is quite small by historical standards and should not be a major source of weakness in our currency.
[ Translation]
The flow of long-term capital funds, which are the source of funds to finance most private sector investments, has continued to favour Canada in 1985; acquisitions of shares of Canadian companies by non-residents were particularly strong. Direct foreign investments in Canada were also high even though they were offset by take-overs of foreign companies by Canadian interests.
In all likelihood the flow of long-term capital funds will continue to have a positive impact on the value of our dollar this year.

It is the typically volatile short-term capital flows which have been influencing our dollar adversely in recent weeks. This speculative activity has arisen from misconceptions about the state of our economy and about the Government's commitment to pursue the policies required to sustain the strong recovery we are now experiencing.
I believe that negative speculation about the Canadian dollar has gone too far. Levels of the exchange rate earlier this week have been clearly below what is justified by fundamental developments in our balance of payments and have not reflected the healthy state of our over-all economic performance. A continuation of this negative sentiment would threaten to undermine the progress we have made in sustaining an economic recovery through strong growth, accompanied by continued moderation in inflation.
The fundamental strength of our economy is reflected in an underlying balance of payments structure that is good. I believe that the speculative elements which I cited that are
countering these fundamental forces will wither away as the sources of that strength are more generally recognized.

The downward pressures on the Canadian dollar in recent months have been offset through foreign exchange market interventions financed with the Government's exchange account and through a gradual increase in short-term interest rates. Still the increase was significant and the gap between our short-term interest rates and those of the United States has widened considerably, more than 3 per cent.

In recent days pressures against the Canadian dollar greatly intensified. To counter unwarranted speculative activity, the Bank of Canada has this week operated forcefully in the domestic money market and, as fiscal agent for the Government of Canada, forcefully in the foreign exchange market. The result has been a strengthening of the Canadian dollar and a sharp further upward movement in short-term interest rates. Our dollar has moved from a low of 69.13 U.S. cents on Tuesday to about 71 cents currently. Today's bank rate has risen to 11.7 per cent, up 67 basis points from last week.
The Government is prepared to continue to reinforce its intervention in the foreign exchange market in order to promote orderly conditions. To this end, yesterday I announced actions which have been taken to increase our reserves of U.S. dollars by $2.4 billion. The Government is prepared to use these official reserves to enter the market as aggressively as necessary to counter speculative pressure on the dollar.
The main purpose of these actions in the financial and exchange markets is to reinforce the thrust of our broad economic policy stance which looks to a continuation of noninflationary growth. To that end fiscal policy will ensure a measured, orderly and significant reduction in our deficit.
I have heard and read in the media many commentaries expressing doubt about the future course of our fiscal policy. These doubts are unwarranted. I have reiterated on many occasions our resolve to improve our fiscal position. This is being done in a comprehensive way and primarily through a reduction in the level of Government spending. The unprecedented spending reductions announced in November, 1984 and in May, 1985 are being implemented and will have a growing fiscal impact over time. Our deficit is under control and it will come down. Monetary policy will continue to be directed at keeping inflation under control. The Government has also moved in other areas, such as energy and foreign investment, to improve the efficiency of our markets and increase confidence in Canada. Together these policies will serve to ensure the sustainability of the recovery and, with it, a strong and stable currency and a return to lower levels of interest rates.

Hear, hear!
[ Translation]

Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I simply cannot understand why the


Minister came to the House this afternoon to deliver that statement.
Indeed, I listened closely, I read the statement carefully and I can tell you that it is nothing to write home about.

The Minister has described what is almost an Agatha Christie mystery-who killed the Canadian dollar? It does not take Hercule Poirot to solve this mystery. The Minister has recited a number of interesting facts about the Canadian economy. I will come to them in a moment, because we have to eliminate each of them as villains in this piece one by one. However, there is one glaring omission, there is one suspect to which reference has not been made. All he has to do is look around him, especially at his Leader, at his Cabinet and from time to time in the mirror, and he will find the cause of the falling Canadian dollar. He will see the killer face to face. [Translation]
The reason-and I will prove it this afternoon-is that there is an obvious lack of coherence in leadership among the Conservatives. We know full well there is political infighting among Cabinet Ministers themselves and especially among caucus members. In short, Mr. Speaker, Canadians and foreigners alike have lost confidence in this Government. [English]
That is what has killed the Canadian dollar.
Let us look for a moment at what he has told us. I read his speech carefully. He takes on the issue of Canada being perceived as a resource exporter and says that there is no reason for people to be alarmed about falling commodity prices or falling oil prices, that that should not be the reason for the fall of the Canadian dollar. Of course he is absolutely right. Most people know that. Unfortunately the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) does not know that. I hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has had the opportunity of educating the Prime Minister who, in an interview in Fortune magazine on March 4, 1985, said the following:
We do not have a very good track record. Our products have not been of the highest quality. Our deliveries have been lacking in reliability. Our expertise has been in large measure borrowed. Our technology has been purchased. What the hell makes us so special? If somebody wants to buy some oil, somebody wants to buy some wheat, hell, we're in the business. That's what it's all about. Forest products, mining-God, we'd love it if somebody wanted to joint-venture with us in mining development, taking our products at competitive prices. Damn right we would.
That is our Prime Minister, of course, spreading that perception. As I say, fortunately, his ignorance is not widespread amongst intelligent members of the business investment communities, and, in fact, among Canadians in general who realize that Canada has become a strong exporter in other areas.
Notwithstanding the efforts of the Prime Minister to denigrate the strength of our export sector, I suggest to you that that is not the villain, it is not that perception. What on earth can it be? Not our rate of inflation says the Minister of Finance. Again, he is absolutely right. The rate of inflation has
Statements by Ministers
hovered around 4 per cent. I might add, the Minister could have recognized that a legacy he received in that "bare cupboard" he likes to refer to was a rate of inflation below 5 per cent, having been brought down by the Liberal Government from something like 12.5 per cent in 1982 through the six and five program to less than 6 per cent in 1983, and less than 5 per cent in 1984. I would like him to acknowledge that some time. I am sure he will.
In addition to that, I need not refer again to the fact, with which we are all painfully familiar, that he received a dollar which had a U.S. exchange rate in September, 1984 of approximately 77 cents, and of course early this week we saw it as low as 69 cents.
Well, he tells us it's not inflation, it's not Gross National Product. We have had sustained growth, so it is not the resource sector, it is not inflation, it is not our Gross National Product that has driven it down. It certianly is not our current account deficit, which he points out is small by historical standards. No reason to be concerned, so it cannot be that. We gradually go through everyone and we finally get to the butler.
In any case, none of these are villains in this piece. Longterm capital flows, the Minister rules that out. Again, we agree with him. Yes, indeed, there must be something else. We have not yet found the killer of the Canadian dollar in all this information which he offered to us here this afternoon. Well, he tells us that there has been this speculation in recent weeks, or even in recent days. Why is that? Why, if we are so strong in all these areas that the Minister describes is the dollar being killed? Why did the Minister have to borrow $2.4 billion yesterday at a cost, as I raised in Question Period, if those loans went to maturity in present value, as high as close to a billion dollars out of Canadian taxpayers' pockets? Why does he have to watch interest rates escalate two-thirds of a point today? He is shaking his head. I will look forward to having him produce the numbers I have got mine here. You can't borrow $2.4 billion for ten years at 9 per cent U.S. without incurring major interest costs. Why is that? Why is that interest rates again today had to increase to 11.47, an increase of .67 cents from yesterday?
I come back to my point, we have eliminated all of the suspects, except one, and that one is right over there on the Government benches, the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister and those other Ministers responsible for economic policy in this country. Let me explain why. Let me offer you the proof very quickly, Mr. Speaker, so this will not simply be treated as partisan rhetoric coming from the Official Opposition. Let's play detective for a moment.
Despite the rhetoric there has been incoherence, there has been confusion, and there has been conflict in our economic policy. I will terminate by offering some quick but convincing evidence. First of all, the Minister of Finance on March 1, 1985 said on CTV "Question Period": "We are going to get the deficit down. We are not going to do it through taxes, there is enough room on the expenditure side". And then a scant two months later he brought in the biggest tax increase


Statements by Ministers
in Canadian history. Now, talk about that in terms of conflict and confusion.
Second, at the same time he brought in a capital gains tax exemption which we had to adopt several weeks ago in this House, there was a measure intended to put capital into Canadian industry, especially the small and medium-sized business sectors. But it was completely unfocused. Where has that money been invested? It was an invitation to divest, and probably reinvest outside Canada. Combine that with the most remarkable suggestion of all, this alternative minimum tax which penalizes recipients of Canadian dividend income and, in fact, required Canadians who had capital tied up in holding companies to divest their assets before year end. Where do you think those moneys were invested, with the prospect of a penalizing tax on Canadian dividend income? To the United States, that is where a lot of that money went. Complete incoherence and confusion.
I am coming quickly to the end, Mr. Speaker, if you will just bear with me because, I do not want the Opposition to think that this is empty rhetoric. I want the Government to reflect on these points, because they stand out so clearly.
The great privatizers, Mr. Speaker. They told the world they were going to privatize. The first major act was the acquisition of a lot of service stations through Petro-Canada, which are found in your province. I know it may have been difficult for you to go back to your riding for some weeks, but I gather the dust is settling down. Privatization the purchase of retail gas stations. Then to counter that perception there has been unseemly haste to dismantle the Canadian aerospace sector and dispose of de Havilland. There has been the attempt to reduce the deficit with excessive tax increases, and perhaps to cover the $2 billion to bail out chartered banks. We have seen the Western Accord which gave hundreds of millions of dollars to multinational oil companies. People do not believe this Government, and with good reason.
So I conclude the killer is before you. The evidence stands. It is not the economy, it is the lack of credibility and confidence in the economic management of this country by this Government.

Mr. Speaker, first I would like to comment briefly on today's decision concerning yet another increase in Canadian interest rates. This policy of the Conservative Government is a threat to Canada and all Canadians. This latest increase in interest rates will likely trigger a sharp rise in bank rates, and if the banks do make that decision, within a month we will have higher interest rates, perhaps up by 2 or 2.5 per cent. It is not good for farmers, it is not good for families about to renegotiate mortgages, and it is not good for the unemployed seeking work. This policy to raise interest rates and shore up the dollar did not work for the Liberals in the past and it is not going to work now.

I want to say, Mr. Speaker, the statement the Minister has made today can be accounted for very largely by, not the ongoing problem of the dollar, but the very large increase in the interest rate that was announced earlier, the two-thirds of a point increase in today's announcement which, when translated by the banks, as it likely will be, will mean that in the past month of this Conservative Government we will have seen an increase in interest rates anywhere from 2 per cent to 2.5 per cent. I say to the Minister that that type of policy was disastrous for farmers, disastrous for homeowners and disastrous for the unemployed when the Liberals implemented it a few years ago. It is no better today when coming from the Conservatives.
Hear, hear!

This is what the interest rate policy announcement will mean in concrete terms. According to the present Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens), when he sat on this side of the House as opposition critic for DREE, he said that a 1 per cent increase in the interest rate-and we almost had that today, and it will likely be 2.5 per cent by the end of the month-means the loss of 25,000 jobs. According to the Hon. Member's calculation then, that means some 50,000 jobs have been placed in jeopardy by the Government's incompetence just in the past month. This monthly increase in interest rates-and I have spoken to my colleagues about it-in terms of the present level of the debt will probably increase farmers' debt charges by about $500 million in one year. Who will pay that? I will tell Hon. Members who will pay. It will be the farm families who will have to pay that increase in debt charges.
I already mentioned earlier today what this increase will mean in terms of mortgage rate changes. Over the life of a mortgage it will cost the typical Canadian family some $12,000. This reassuring the-land-is-strong type of statement which we heard from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) will not fool Canadians. Canadians will note that the most significant announcement today came not from the Government of Canada but from the Bank of Canada, sanctioned by the Government. I refer to the announcement with respect to the increase in interest rates. The Minister opposed that policy when he sat on this side of the House and he ought not to be supporting it now that he is in Government.
Hear, hear!

In our view the Minister has correctly said that some of the recent problems with respect to the dollar are to be attributed to speculators in Chicago and elsewhere. I think there is certainly evidence to support that. I hope that in that context the Government has communicated with the Government of the United States to see if anything can be done through regulatory mechanisms to head off this speculation which puts the whole country in a hostage situation as a result of the operations of a handful of speculators. I doubt


that anything can be done. However, I hope the Canadian Government has made some inquiries to see if anything can be done. The Minister is right, speculators have played a role.
It is also the case that the great fluctuation in energy prices has played a role. I also want to say that it was the Minister's Party, and his Government, which deregulated the oil industry. They said that it has to be left open to the whims of the market-place and, therefore, if we are now having to react to what the Saudi Arabians have decided in a completely unfettered way, once again it is his Government's decision that has placed us in this type of precarious situation.
Quite apart from the short-run questions there are some longer-range problems which the Minister did not discuss and to which he alluded in a rather oblique way. One of these concerns the flow of investment. Yesterday, the Minister and I had an exchange in the House about what has gone on in the 12 months since his Party formed the Government. I wish to make the point again today, and perhaps the Minister on another occasion will deal with it. I would like to look at what happened in Canada between the last quarter of 1984 and the last quarter of 1985. I wish to begin by conceding with regard to what the Minister said yesterday. Yes, there was an 11 per cent increase in investment in Canada. That is true, and we are pleased to see it. As I have also said to the Minister on another occasion, it is true that our job forecasts were inaccurate and that the economy performed in a better way than we had anticipated. More jobs were produced. I have always taken it as a matter of principle that when the Government does something right we should say so. If something turns out to be better than we had estimated, then we should also say so. The Minister is now smiling because I agree.
Oh, oh!

I now wish to see what he will say. He pointed out that there was an 11 per cent increase in investment in the Canadian economy last year. What is decisive in terms of its impact on the dollar is not that increase. What is decisive is that there was a 44 per cent increase in money leaving the country for investment. That is what impacts on the dollar. So we had an 11 per cent increase in terms of new investment and in terms of job creation, which is good, but a 44 per cent increase-some $5.2 billion-leaving the country to create jobs elsewhere. I also want to say to the Minister, as he well understands, that this drives the Canadian dollar down. What we need are policies which will keep that investment in Canada. Let the Minister deal with that issue.
Hear, hear!

I wish to say to the Minister-who is again smiling-I hope that he will deal with the issue of that 44 per cent increase year-over-year. If we look at what was going on in 1985, after the Minister tabled his Budget last spring, we will see that the flow of investment abroad actually accelerated. Thus, if his Budget had any effect on investment intentions it was to say to Canadians: "Take your money and run with it out of the country". The Minister ought to be reassessing some
Statements by Ministers
of his policies in a serious way in terms of his forthcoming Budget.
The second matter I wish to point out is that we are dealing not only with a current crisis in terms of the dollar but, as the Minister knows, for a number of years the Canadian dollar has been at a pretty low level. There are some serious structural explanations for that. One of them is the high degree of foreign ownership. The Minister will recall the time just about a month ago, around the end of the year, when there were transfers of massive sums of money from Canada largely to the United States. We had another kind of run on the dollar- another dip in the dollar. Why? Because the branch plants were making their dividend payments back home; or we were making payments for service charges. If the Minister were to look at some of the numbers he would be somewhat concerned because they are quite disturbing. The most recent figures we have in this respect are for 1984. We do not yet have the figures for 1985. The figures for 1984 are as follows. We paid out some $3.2 billion in dividend charges. That had a negative effect on the Canadian dollar. We also paid out some $6 billion in service charges in 1984. No doubt this pattern will continue for 1985.
I wish to say to the Minister, and to my Liberal colleagues, that it is this type of strutural problem about which the New Democratic Party has been concerned for years. It is not because American investors are the bad guys, or any other foreigner is a bad guy, a bad woman or a bad company. We say that it is bad for the Canadian economy to have that level of foreign ownership-

I am amazed that the Government is proceeding to impose an 11 per cent tax on such items as surgical gloves, sutures, surgical equipment, needles and syringes. This will increase the operating costs of our hospitals so that, on the one hand, the Government is cutting back on transfer payments, squeezing our health care system and hospitals in particular while, on the other hand, it is extracting more money from them by imposing this new tax. In other words, the Government is really taxing itself.
One must assume that there must be sane people on the Government benches, but it just does not make any sense for them to take such action.
The Conservative Party, whose Leader John Diefenbaker took great pride in helping to establish medicare in this country, is nickel and diming our medicare system to death. Such a move is outrageous and defies logic or any sense of compassion and reasonableness.
Furthermore, there will be a new 11 per cent tax on non-prescription drugs and health care products such as vitamins which are an important supplement to the diet of many people, particularly older people. There will be an 11 per cent tax on aspirin which is used by many Canadians, particularly older people.
Many doctors prescribe aspirin, yet the Government is intent on imposing an 11 per cent tax on that product. Cough syrup, cold remedies and medicated shampoos are examples of other products that will be taxed. While these products may not require a prescription, they are health products which are essential to the health and well-being of some people.
This does not seem to matter to the Government. These products will be taxed by another 11 per cent. In other words, we now have a tax on illness. The Government wants to make a profit on sick people.

This is a new industry that has emerged in less than 10 years, mostly as a result of the initiatives taken by the then Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, Alistair Gillespie, following the oil price crisis.
I am told also that the potential in the world for the absorption of equipment, material and technology of this kind is somewhere in the neighbourhood of $4 billion, which is not a minor amount. It has enormous export potential for Canadian entrepreneurs and Canadian workers.
In support of this motion as well I would like to say a couple of words which I did not express at second reading in relation to the position of taxes on gasoline. At that time, you may recall, I was very upset by the fact that the application of taxation on gasoline, as it is proposed in Bill C-80, is one that has serious environmental consequences. I am glad to see the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) in the House today because it may have some relevance to his way of thinking. The tax that is being proposed in this Bill on unleaded gasoline is greater than on leaded gasoline. Therefore, once this becomes law, the price at the pump will be affected so that the gap in price at the retail level will be greater than it is now. As Hon. Members must have noticed there is now a three-cent gap, more or less, at gas pumps across the country. Some six months ago it was 2.59 cents. I am afraid that with the imposition of this measure the gap will increase. Of course, this move will cause two negative consequences. The first is with respect to misfueling. Those people who buy leaded gasoline, who really should be buying unlead-


Excise Tax Act
ed gasoline, will be encouraged to misuse gasoline. Second, the greater consumption of leaded gas will lead to undesirable health problems, as Hon. Members well know. In addition, the use of unleaded gasoline is possible in cars which are equipped with catalytic converters. Catalytic converters are gadgets which reduce the emissions of nitrous oxide into the environment. Accordingly, the acidity of the rain is reduced and the environment is protected. Therefore, it is necessary to impress upon the Minister of Finance and the Government the notion that the imposition of a tax on gasoline which is greater on unleaded than on leaded gasoline is environmentally wrong.
I carry the argument further by suggesting that we introduce a tax system on gasoline which is so adjusted that the prices for the two at gasoline pumps are equal. This has been done in some European countries, in particular Austria. It is a desirable and ultimately possible goal.
I realize that in this regard there may be some difficulties encountered by farmers and fishermen. In the past their concerns have been taken into account through the use of programs which have refunded them the difference between the amount they have paid and what they would have paid under an existing regime. Something of this nature could be put into place with respect to unleaded and leaded gasoline as well.
From an environmental point of view, I repeat, it is undesirable to sell leaded gasoline at a price lower than that charged for unleaded gasoline. There is no doubt about that. On the one hand, there is an increase in the demand for automobiles running on leaded gasoline. On the other hand, this move provides an incentive for the misfueling of automobiles designed to run on unleaded gasoline. I know that the Minister of the Environment has been quite articulate on this matter. He has not only expressed his concern, but I am sure that he has also put pressure on his provincial colleagues to find ways of discouraging and possibly eliminating this type of practice which is damaging to the environment.
The matter boils down to this. The price advantage leads to increased lead pollution, when there is a price advantage in terms of leaded gasoline. It also leads to acid rain-causing emissions. That is really the bottom line. It is therefore desirable that we use the federal commodity tax system to eliminate this price advantage. It is important from now on when we approach the taxation of gasoline that we do so with a political concern for the damage caused by acid rain in this very particular daily manner. It is important that our taxation structure reflect this concern. This is a departure from past practices. We have come to this conclusion as a result of the experiences of a number of other countries, particularly in Europe, which suffer acid rain damage because of dense vehicular traffic in highly populated areas.
I submit that it would be to our long-term benefit if we could put into place a gasoline taxation structure whereby unleaded gasoline is made available to the consumer at the same price as leaded gasoline for the reasons I have mentioned
earlier. In so doing we would reduce the lead emissions and the concomitant health dangers accompanying those emissions. This would apply particularly to our urban areas where the emissions of nitrous oxide, which are emissions caused typically by the combustion engine process, find their way into the atmosphere and come back to us in the form of acid rain. It is with this in mind that I make this intervention.
I do so in the hope that in the little time left between report stage and the conclusion of third reading stage and the time which will be required for the examination of the Bill in the Senate that the Government will see fit to introduce a modification to the specific rate of sales tax imposed on this petroleum product. A specific increase on leaded gasoline will be required so as to permit unleaded gasoline to find its way to the dump at price equal to that of leaded gasoline. I am sure you, Mr. Speaker, your children and your grandchildren would substantially benefit, as all of us would and will, if this so-called Progressive Conservative Government, which is neither progressive nor really conservative when it comes to matters of this type, will see the light and adopt a conservation measure which in the end will benefit the health of all Canadians. In the end it will also benefit the health, growth and quality of our forests because, as Hon. Members know, acid rain is an issue of health and an issue of the growth and good quality of our basic natural resources.

PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   JUDICIAL APPOINTMENTS ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-259, an Act to amend the Federal Court Act, the Northwest Territories Act, the Supreme Court Act, the Tax Court of Canada Act and the Yukon Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased indeed to have this opportunity to move second reading of Bill C-259, and to move as well that the Bill be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs for consideration.
This Bill is being put forward at this time with a view to establishing a process for the parliamentary scrutiny of all federal judicial appointments. Now, I wish that that were a simple matter and we could put that forward in one Bill, or in one motion, but it is not quite that easy, I am told. The difficulty lies in the fact that appointments are made to a number of federal courts by the Governor in Council under a number of different federal Acts. Those are the Acts that I referred to in Bill C-259 that is before us today: the Federal Court Act, the Northwest Territories Act, the Supreme Court Act, the Tax Court of Canada Act and the Yukon Act.
In addition to that, there are other appointments made by the Governor in Council, but those, however, are made under Section 96 of the Constitution Act. Because of that fact it is necessary, in order to establish a judicial review procedure or a
Judicial Appointments Act
parliamentary review procedure, for appointments of that sort-and those, by the way, are appointments to Superior, County and District Courts in the provinces-to be made by way of constitutional amendment to set up a similar procedure. That is why my Bill, while it deals with the five different pieces of federal legislation, does not, in fact, deal with an amendment to the Constitution Act. That would require a constitutional amendment, and that is going to be dealt with separately because I have placed on the Order Paper a Notice of Motion No. 252 which reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of undertaking negotiations with the provincial governments to establish a process for the parliamentary scrutiny of federal judicial appointments made under section 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867, in order to ensure that in making these appointments, the government is guided by the highest standards of conduct.
That motion will come forward at a separate time and it will give us another opportunity to debate this matter.
Of course I hope the Hon. Members will see fit to pass my Bill at second reading stage and move it on to committee today. Both the Bill and the motion provide for the parliamentary scrutiny of all federal judicial appointments. Let me quote the following statement: "That, in my view, is a necessity in order to reinforce public trust that all judicial appointments are of the highest calibre and that in making those appointments the Government is guided by the highest standards of conduct". I am quoting here directly from a comment made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on September 9 of last year when he introduced his seven points on public ethics and used those very words to describe the process that he hoped this House would adopt.
Now you will remember that during the 1984 federal election campaign, Government patronage appointments, and particularly judicial appointments, were a major issue. Just before he handed over power to former Prime Minister Turner the then former Prime Minister Trudeau reached an agreement with Mr. Turner that there would be certain patronage appointments made. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), as he now is, agreed that there would be certain patronage appointments made, including a number of judicial appointments. Subsequently those appointments were made, and that touched off a controversy that gripped the country during the last federal election campaign, a controversy which, as we all know, is renewed in this House every time the Government makes an appointment of any sort.
The total issue of course is one that is much wider than merely that of judicial appointments; it covers all Government appointments. You will recall, as I said a few moments ago, that our present Prime Minister addressed the topic of Government appointments as part of his statement concerning standards of conduct required by the Government and the Public Service that he delivered in this House on September 9, 1985. In that statement the Prime Minister dealt with a package of seven major initiatives on public sector ethics. They included an experimental program of parliamentary scrutiny of Governor in Council appointments, and that, of course, is part of the package of reforms that is now before the House, is being


Judicial Appointments Act
considered, and hopefully will be approved very shortly by everyone in this House.
In addition to that package of seven initiatives there was also included a review of the judicial appointment process. In his statement the Prime Minister announced that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) had the judicial appointment process under active review. Well, of course it is still under active review and we have not had a report back from the Minister of Justice on that subject as yet. That is what Bill C-259 is all about, it is to bring forward a process for that form of review of judicial appointments.
In introducing this Bill I do not want to leave the impression that I question the competence or the integrity of our judges. The country has been and continues to be well served by its judges. However, I am introducing this Bill because I share a concern that was expressed by the committee of the Canadian Bar Association on the independence of the judiciary, which reported in August of last year and indicated that the existence of political influence in judicial appointments could undermine public confidence in the judicial system. At the same time it reported that Canadians are cynical about the current method of appointing judges and want a totally different method. I agree with those statements, and I also agree with the statement of the Chief Justice of Canada that was made a year earlier, in August of 1984-actually during the election campaign of 1984-when he said that, "the public is entitled to be reassured that our judges are appointed on the basis of merit and legal excellence alone". That is really what I am trying to accomplish in introducing this Bill C-259.
At the moment we have a process of federal judicial appointments that is behind the curtains, if you will. It is something that goes on away from public view. In fact, the Governor in Council can make some 760 federal appointments. There are some 760 federally appointed judges at the present time. The Governor in Council makes those appointments to the Federal Court; the courts of the Northwest Territories, the courts of the Yukon, the Tax Court of Canada, the Supreme Court of Canada, and also, as I indicated under Section 96 of the Constitution Act, appoint Superior District and County Court judges in each province, except for the Courts of Probate in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
In actual practice what goes on is that the Minister of Justice has the responsibility for recommending to the Governor in Council the persons who should be considered for this sort of judicial appointment. The appointment of the Chief Justice actually rests with the Prime Minister, but in all cases except, as I understand it, in cases of Supreme Court of Canada appointments, it is actually the Minister of Justice who performs this duty on behalf of the Prime Minister.
In actual practice, however, it is an official, of course, in the Department of Justice who does this sort of thing. He gathers suggestions from far and wide across the country through a network of persons, including judges, lawyers, law schools, Members of Parliament and provincial officials. Once he has a tentative choice for a candidate, that candidate's name is submitted to the national committee on the judiciary of the
Canadian Bar Association. This committee then evaluates the suggested candidate and reports back to the Department its opinion as to whether this person is well qualified, qualified or not qualified enough.
Although political patronage in judicial appointments has declined over the years, it is obvious that it has not disappeared altogether. Of course, during the past election campaign there were appointments announced. They were announced without the advice of the national committee on the judiciary having been sought. That is what this Bill is aimed at trying to eliminate. We are trying to set up a process of openness so that every appointment will have the opportunity of being publicly vetted. There have been a good many suggestions as to how this should be done.
In our country, from 1956 through until 1979 I believe, there were some four different suggestions put forward as to how we should go about this. All of them involved some aspect of having provincial input into the selection of judges for the Supreme Court of Canada. In the summer of 1985, the Canadian Bar Association proposed a more comprehensive system on the topic of the independence of the judiciary. It proposed that an advisory committee be set up to seek candidates and to assess their qualifications. It also proposed that this committee be composed of judges, lawyers, representatives appointed by the federal and provincial Justice Ministers or Attorneys General, and members of the public. The Government would then be able to choose the best qualified from among those candidates. It is interesting to note that the committee did not advocate a parliamentary review of judicial appointments as my Bill proposes.
The Americans, of course, have adopted a process of having a Congressional or Senate review of judicial appointments. Some American judges are elected and some are appointed by state Governors. However, federal judicial appointments are made by the President with something that is called the advice and consent of the Senate. This means that while the President formally nominates a candidate for a judicial appointment, the matter is investigated by the Attorney General of the United States, by the standing committee on the federal judiciary of the American Bar Association, and then by the Senate judiciary committee, which reviews all nominations to the federal bench in the United States and which makes the ultimate recommendation to the Senate.
What I propose is not exactly an American-type of legislative review. Of course, it is one model which we could look to. There are also other models we could look to. What I am suggesting is a model of parliamentary review which, in fact, is already in use in Canada. While it is not a procedure which may be familiar to most Hon. Members, it is a procedure which is set out in a strange Act of Parliament entitled the Safe Containers Convention Act. It is an Act of Parliament, much to the surprise of most, I suspect which sets out exactly the same method I propose in my Bill.


The Act provides that where there is a recommendation made by the Governor in Council, or an order for a judicial appointment, that recommendation must be tabled in each of the Houses of Parliament within five days of the making of the order. The order is then referred to a committee of the House of Commons or of the Senate. The committee has the opportunity to review the appointment and report back to the House of Commons or the Senate within 30 days of receiving the order. If it is not reported back in 30 days, then the order is confirmed and the appointment is made. If it is reported back negatively, then Members of the House of Commons or the Senate are given the opportunity to place before the House a notice of motion, which is to be signed by either 25 Members of Parliament or 15 Senators, depending on which House deals with the matter, asking for a debate on the particular appointment. The debate has to follow within five days of the tabling of the notice of motion and is limited to five hours. If the motion is defeated, then the appointment goes through. If the motion is passed, then the matter is referred to the other place, be it the Senate or the House of Commons, and within five days of receiving the motion it must be debated by that place. There is also a five-hour time limit placed on debate. If it fails in that House, then the appointment goes through. However, if it passes, then the appointment is rejected. That is the procedure that I suggest in my Bill. It may not be a familiar procedure to most of us, but it is a procedure that is already in place. In that sense it is not something new or foreign. This is why I feel it is appropriate in this instance.
As I have indicated, the Canadian Bar Association does not recommend this method. It suggests the formation of an advisory committee of the bar association itself. The interesting thing I have noted is that in the United States there is an advisory committee of the American Bar Association. If the late President Woodrow Wilson had always accepted the advice of the bar association's judicial committee with respect to who should be nominated to the Supreme Court of the United States, then Mr. Justice Brandeis, a well known and respected jurist, would never have been selected since he was not recommended by the American Bar Association.
In my view, this reinforces the need for Canada to have an open process of parliamentary review for these judicial appointments. Basically, that is what I am saying in my Bill. I am saying that we should have a public scrutiny process. It is the only way by which we can reassure the public that this major concern which arose in the last election campaign can be dealt with properly. In this way we can reassure Canadians generally that all judicial appointments will be of the highest calibre and that in making appointments the Government will be guided by the highest standards of conduct. That is the basic thrust of my Bill.
It is with that in mind that I commended to the House that this Bill be given second reading and reference to a legislative committee. I hope that Members of the House will agree to my proposal for no other reason than to give us an opportunity to discuss the question of some sort of review or a new process for judicial appointments.
Judicial Appointments Act

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   JUDICIAL APPOINTMENTS ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in this debate and 1 have to say to the House that it is unfortunate that we do not have all the time required to debate the value and substance of this Bill C-259, an Act to amend the Federal Court Act, the Northwest Territories Act, the Supreme Court Act, the Tax Court of Canada Act and the Yukon Act.
At the outset, Mr. Speaker, may I commend the Hon. Member for this initiative which is excellent and quite timely indeed because it relates to something which is important to me, namely the parliamentary scrutiny of appointments to the various courts of the land.
Mr. Speaker, parliamentary scrutiny and review of such appointments is necessary if only because in most instances nowadays it is based on a system which is not only archaic but which in many cases does not quite reflect true democracy, which means public review and scrutiny of those appointments.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw your attention to a simple case which I have been mentioning in the House these past few days, as Hon. Members would know, and of course I am talking about the appointment of a bilingual Francophone judge to the Ontario Court of Appeal. It is unfortunate that this incident could not have been settled through the parliamentary process. I am certain that this House, for example, if it had to vote on the appointment of a judge in Ontario today, knowing full well that there are 500,000 Franco-Ontarians in this province, knowing full well that the provincial legislature passed a law in 1984 which was proclaimed in 1985 and which will be in force throughout the province in 1986, it would keep in mind the fact that Franco-Ontarians, like all other Francophones who come here from elsewhere in Canada, might have access to the courts in their own language. That is not what happened, Mr. Speaker, and it is unfortunate bcause we, as Parliamentarians, did not have the right to examine the appointment and to check the qualifications of the appointee, especially as concerns the linguistic criteria, which should always be kept in mind.
Mr. Speaker, I could read the correspondence of Mr. Robert Paris, for instance, the former president of the French-speaking jurists of Ontario, who recommends parliamentary review and examination of the linguistic qualifications of judges appointed to superior and appeals courts.
However, my time is limited and I want to leave my colleague of the New Democratic Party enough time to say a few words. Since we do not have much time and we do not have all the . . . Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that of the 16 judges of the Ontario Appeals Court, only two can speak French.
At the Quebec Appeals Court, there are also 16 judges, but they are all bilingual, and 8 of them, if I recall correctly, it is


Judicial Appointments Act
in fact 18. Yes, 1 am sorry, but it is 18. Of these 18 judges, 8 are bilingual anglophones.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the House could agree to something as simple as a review to ensure equity in these appointments to the courts. I do not think that it is too much to ask that these appointments be submitted to the Canadian Parliament to ensure linguistic equity in this country.
Mr. Speaker, I could give you the names of the judges in New Brunswick, where the proportion is fifty-fifty, in Quebec, in Ontario and elsewhere, but that is not the point. I think that the Hon. Member tried to make us aware of the need to implement a new mechanism for appointments which would require a review of judicial appointments by Parliament, meaning both the House of Commons and the Senate.
Before resuming my seat, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member once more and tell the House that what is at issue here is not the legal ability of the judges. I do not know that much about it as I am not a lawyer myself. However, I do know that if I go before the courts in Ontario and I want to speak French, it is essential that the judge be able to speak my language.
When the House adopted Bill C-42 a few years ago, it accepted the principle whereby each Canadian has the right in this country to be heard by a judge speaking his or her own language. I suggest that is a basic right. I just cannot accept the fact that because only two cases were heard last year in Ontario out of 1,400, it is a good enough reason for disregarding the linguistic aspect.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that a right cannot be quantified, that it is wrong to do so and that a right must apply to everybody. As a Parliamentarian, Mr. Speaker, I feel, as I am sure a great many of my colleagues do, that it is high time for the Government to submit its appointments to a parliamentary review and that this would be a major step for democracy in the country.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   JUDICIAL APPOINTMENTS ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that we only have five minutes. In order to let other Hon. Members speak, I will be brief. It is unfortunate that we do not have much time because it is a very interesting Bill. It is a good Bill and I support it in principle. I have some questions about the procedure of applying the Safe Container Convention Act to judges. That is a new one, but it is very imaginative. I did not realize that procedure was there. It is a procedure for House scrutiny.
The Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), the justice critic of the New Democratic Party, has in the past supported scrutiny of appointments, especially judicial appointments, by the House. I hope that a technically good way can be found to do that.
I regret it only applies to the federal courts and not to the Superior Courts in the provinces where the real judging goes on. If I had my way, I would almost abolish federal courts because I think we could have a much simpler system of justice if we ran them in with the provincial courts on the superior level.
I think this is overdue because of new laws like the Charter of Rights. We are asking a lot more from our judges. We are asking for high calibre and that they be completely unbiased. We expect them to be really quite extraordinary people, and many of our judges are extraordinary people.
I hope that judges come from other parts of society as well. I think we need more women on the bench. I would like to see some community lawyers on the bench, not just corporate lawyers. We need people who have been out in the world. That is what we will need for interpretation of the new Charter of Rights.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   JUDICIAL APPOINTMENTS ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I too would like to congratulate my colleague, the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway), for bringing this subject before Parliament. There has been considerable discussion about the appointment of judges and I think it is an important issue for Parliamentarians to look at. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), in his discussion of the appointment of judges, raised a specific example. He referred specifically to the recent appointment of a judge in the province of Ontario and questioned the process by which that appointment was made. It is important to look at the facts of just who the judges are and who have been appointed in the province of Ontario since that issue is now before Parliament.
At the District Court level in the province of Ontario, there are 146 judges, 15 per cent of whom are bilingual. On the Supreme Court level, there are 18 judges at the appeal level, three of whom, not two, are bilingual. The Chief Justice of Ontario himself has said that there is no problem with bilingual trials or appeals.
The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier says he is talking as a Parliamentarian. Well, I can say to you, Mr. Speaker, that as a Parliamentarian, he is doing a disservice to his province and to his country by injecting this matter into Parliament again and again since this appointment.
Bill C-259, the Judicial Appointments Bill, which was introduced by my colleague, raises a number of interesting points. It does not purport to cover all judicial appointments in Canada. In fact, I believe it covers just 50 out of the over 700 appointments which are made by the federal Government. It excludes those who are appointed under Section 96 of the British North America Act. My colleague said perhaps there would be constitutional difficulties. It would be an interesting case to have referred to the Supreme Court of Canada in order to see whether in fact a Bill such as the type introduced by my colleague could, in fact, be made and not have it ruled unconstitutional. In any case, the Bill deals exclusively with appointments to the so-called Section 101 Courts, which are the Supreme Court of Canada, the Federal Court, the Tax


Court and the Supreme Courts of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. In order to accomplish the purpose of this Bill, the method of appointment to Section 101 Courts would have to be changed. At present there is a considerable variety in the statutory formulae applicable to the appointment of judges to each of those Courts. For instance, while all appointments are made by the Governor in Council, those to the Supreme Court and the Federal Court are by Letters Patent under the Great Seal.

subtopic: ENERGY-MAJOR OIL FIND IN BEAUFORT SEA
ENERGY-MAJOR OIL FIND IN BEAUFORT SEA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reason I am rising this evening is not because I was dissatisfied with the answer given by the Parliamentary Secretary on
Adjournment Debate
January 16. It is because I feel that the discovery of what appeared to be very sizeable oil reserves in the Beaufort Sea is something worthy of comment in this House. It is of extreme importance not only to the part of Canada I have the Honour to represent but to all Canadians.
On December 30 a press release was issued by Gulf Canada Resources announcing that they, in co-operation with their partners in the Amauligak 1-65 well, had been successful. They estimated that the well was capable of producing something like 35,000 barrels of oil a day. Estimates as to the size of the oil pool in the Amauligak structure might be something like 1 billion barrels. To put it into perspective, that is something quite larger than Hibernia.
What does this represent for the North? First of all, it indicates some success for an exploration program which has been going on for many years. It entailed the expenditure of billions and billions of dollars. Credit is due to Dome Petroleum, one of the early major operators in that area. That company developed a lot of technology. While they themselves have not been that successful, Gulf has been, as so often happens in the circumstances. Esso have also been operators in that area. They invested a lot of money and are worthy of comment. We are all pleased to see the success. The effort has paid off.
My constituents in the delta were always very concerned that the exploration effort in that area might dry up. It had been successful in a way in that a lot of oil and gas had been found, but it had been in accumulations that were not big enough to justify the expensive transportation systems that would be needed to bring that oil to southern markets.
Regardless of what happens to the price of oil in the near future, the find now is of such magnitude that the owners thereof cannot walk away from it. Therefore, we can be assured of continued activity in exploration and development in that area for some years to come. We can look forward to the construction of a pipeline down the Mackenzie Valley. There is one there now from Norman Wells in the Territories to Zama in Alberta. If this particular find was put into production, that line would need looping and an extension. There may be need for a brand new line all the way from the delta to refineries in the Edmonton area.
I am pleased to report, Mr. Speaker, that a lot of the preliminary work has already been done. The socio-environmental studies, the economic studies, and the environmental studies have been largely done already. This could proceed expeditiously without getting into the same kind of mix-up we experienced 10 years ago. Exploration is still ongoing, but in the near future we can look forward to the development and production stage. I am pleased to see that legislation has been introduced in the House which gets rid of the old PIP program. If that system had any usefulness, it has now expired. We are looking at a royalty regime and a system of incentives that is more in keeping with the new stage in the production effort in the Beaufort Sea.


Adjournment Debate
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney), in a trip to Inuvik earlier this year, promised to work on a northern accord similar to the Western Accord, a system of revenue sharing to allow the people who live in the Territories to derive immediate benefits from developments as they take place. We need a better system of management than COGLA, which we have at the present time, which reports to two masters. Those are the things which remain to be done.
The last point I would like to make, Mr. Speaker, is that it has always been somewhat embarrassing to people like myself from the Territories who recognize that we take more out of Canada than we put in. It is expensive to operate education and health systems and to build roads there. We are very grateful for the amount of money that southern Canadians have put into the North. However, we look forward to self-sufficiency as a result of oil and gas activity. We look forward to being able to pay our own way in Confederation in the very near future. I think I speak for all of my constituents and all the people in the Territories when I say that we are delighted with this extremely important find which has been made in the Beaufort Sea.

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ENERGY-MAJOR OIL FIND IN BEAUFORT SEA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not often that one has good and exciting news to talk about. I know that my hon. friend from Western Arctic is very proud of his area. I have visited there with him on occasion. The news of the Amauligak discovery was greeted with some joy by everyone, no matter what their political stripe.
In December, 1985, it was announced that a major discovery had been made at 1-65, the first delienation well drilled into the Amauligak structure in the Beaufort Sea. Drilling was carried out from the giant Molikpaq caisson over a sand berm. I was on the Molikpaq last summer and it is quite an exciting and interesting operation. Based on its first two tests, Gulf has stated that oil flowed at rates in excess of 7,000 barrels a day with calculated capacity on the second test of 35,000 barrels a day. Testing has been completed on 1-65 and they are now doing additional drilling at I-65A, and will continue in the coming months. Based on the test results from 1-65 delineation well, it appears to be one of the most productive wells in Canada's history. Needless to say, we are excited about the fact that it is the first indicated commercial discovery in the Beaufort Sea. The Government of Canada shares the industry's enthusiasm about these results. Nevertheless, we do recognize the requirement to undertake further testing and drilling on this structure to determine more precisely the magnitude of the field.
I might add that in the midst of plummeting world oil prices, it is encouraging to note that independent oil analysts have commented that project development of this field should not be impeded by lower international price levels.
The Amauligak well has produced the highest flow rates in the Beaufort Sea in more than a decade. We are hopeful that further drilling will yield more promising results that will
result in Amauligak being the lead project prompting full-scale development in the Beaufort region. Of course, this will do nothing but good for the citizens of the North, especially in the western Arctic which my hon. friend represents so ably.

subtopic: ENERGY-INCREASES IN GASOLINE PRICES. (B) CONSUMER PROTESTS
ENERGY-INCREASES IN GASOLINE PRICES. (B) CONSUMER PROTESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize to my hon. friend, but the Parliamentary Secretary is here and I would like to finish with him. He has certainly earned his keep today and yesterday. He has been here consistently as well as in the committee. I want to make life a little bit more difficult for him.
I rise tonight concerning a question I put to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) on January 20, 1986. Let me quote from page 9943 of Hansard on January 20, 1986:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. On March 28, 1985, on the date we debated the Western Accord, as reported at page 3473 of Hansard the Minister said in the House:
"If the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) is right that by creating a market environment prices will continue to decline, obviously that provides the environment for gasoline prices to decline. They certainly are not going to increase in a declining market."
I asked:
-why are gasoline prices increasing in a declining market? What does the Minister intend to do about it in order to protect the Canadian consumer?
The Minister has received much publicity in the press and is supposed to be one of the stars of the Government. That star has begun to fall in the last couple of weeks.
The question that I asked in the House of Commons is one that every ordinary Canadian motorist is asking. When they read in the paper that the price of oil has dropped from $28 American to $20 American and even lower, they ask why prices have not come down at the gas pumps. Why have Canadian consumers not benefited from this? That is the question I put on behalf of all Canadians. After the NDP kept pressure on for about a week, the Minister finally sent a telex, got down on her knees and prayed to the oil companies to reduce the prices.
We told her that she has the ability at her fingertips to do something about this. She has the power under Canadian law, Section 7(2) of the Petro-Canada Act, to instruct Petro-Canada-since it is our oil company-to lower the prices if the other oil companies will not lower theirs. The Minister said that she could not do that. She could not let Petro-Canada be a price setter, but rather a follower of the other oil companies.
Not only is Petro-Canada following the other oil companies, it is restricting competition for a small business couple in Gravenhurst, Ontario. They wanted to lower the price at their gas station by 2 cents a litre, but the Government oil company threatened to lock their pumps. This is taking place at a time of declining oil prices. That is why there is so much concern. People are angry.


I have had calls and letters from all over the country. Tomorrow we will be tabling a petition from the lower mainland of British Columbia with 3,500 signatures on it. The city council of Powell River, I think, has passed a motion complaining about the increase in gasoline prices. There is a group in Montreal, a spontaneous grass roots group, that has formed to fight the Government on higher oil prices. I am getting phone calls from Toronto, the Maritimes, from everywhere, Mr. Speaker. The Canadian Automobile Association put an advert in the newspaper. From British Columbia we got 1,500 replies in one week. People are angry.
The Parliamentary Secretary said that the Government expected the decline in prices at the retail level to come sooner than expected. Industry competition in the refined product business will come on like gangbusters, he said. Where is it? It has been 62 days since December 6 when the price of oil started moving from $29 to $27 a barrel. The price of gasoline has not come down. We hear that these things are in the pipeline. But we are still waiting.
The Americans have lower gasoline prices. Our problem is too many Government taxes. The Government keeps adding more taxes. The Liberal Government in Quebec did it the other night. The Liberal Government in Ontario was going to do the same thing until the NDP in Ontario stopped it. As well, we have a non-competitive system.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) says the Government needs the money. I do not want to hear this argument from the Hon. gentleman opposite. We hear that the Government needs the money for social services. Why did the Government give $5.3 billion in tax advantages to the oil companies? The people of Canada have said enough is enough. They see oil prices declining. They want the price of gasoline to come down at the pump and they are asking why it has not.

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ENERGY-INCREASES IN GASOLINE PRICES. (B) CONSUMER PROTESTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that was one of the greatest shows I have seen in a long time put on by my friend, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). He has been energy critic for the New Democratic Party for five years. I am surprised the Hon. Member does not understand the energy business any better than what he has apparently shown. The Member does not have a clue how the system works, no idea at all. The Member stands there and says when the price of a barrel of oil goes down today, the prices at the pump should go down today.

subtopic: ENERGY-INCREASES IN GASOLINE PRICES. (B) CONSUMER PROTESTS
speechtext: That is not what I said. Sixty days you said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ENERGY-INCREASES IN GASOLINE PRICES. (B) CONSUMER PROTESTS
speechtext:
Let us make a deal. I sat quietly and listened to the Member's tirade, which was full of nonsense. I could have interrupted him many times. I have only three minutes. The Member had seven minutes, seven minutes too many, I might add.
Let me tell the Hon. Member that it takes 60 days from the time the oil comes from the wellhead to the time it reaches the
Adjournment Debate
market. The Member knows that. He talks about the price of oil after December 9 dropping from $29 to $27 a barrel. There was movement in the market-place at that time. That is when it started the downward trend. The real drop came January 28. The Member admitted this in the House himself the other day. That was a week ago, which means it will not be until the end of March before we see the dramatic drop hit the pumps.
We saw today that Imperial Oil lowered its rack price by 2 cents a litre in Toronto and Sarnia. That is what the free market is all about. When the Hon. Member stands up and quotes figures to the Canadian people, it is no wonder people are confused. The Member is being a little less than honest with Canadians in the way he throws figures around. He knows that. I thought much more of the gentleman because he was energy critic. The Member wanted to be Energy Minister in British Columbia. He volunteered his services. But they did not want him. They wanted him to stay here in Ottawa.

subtopic: ENERGY-INCREASES IN GASOLINE PRICES. (B) CONSUMER PROTESTS
speechtext: Who told you that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ENERGY-INCREASES IN GASOLINE PRICES. (B) CONSUMER PROTESTS
speechtext: If he were honest with Canadians, the Member would explain how the system works. He is taking an issue like this and playing cheap politics with people's lives and with gas prices. Canadians see through that. They understand. They know it takes time. They know that it took 60 days for prices to rise once stock was depleted. The same thing happens when the prices are coming down. We are going to see the results of that. In conclusion, he was critical of the Minister and said that her star is falling. I am going to tell you something, her star is on the rise. She is one of the best energy ministers this country has ever seen, and I predict she is going to be around, I predict, a lot longer than the Hon. Member for Vancouver Kingsway.

subtopic: INSURANCE-LIABILITY COVERAGE (A) DIFFICULTIES FACED BY SMALL BUSINESS. (B) SOLVENCY GUIDELINES FOR INSURANCE COMPANIES
INSURANCE-LIABILITY COVERAGE (A) DIFFICULTIES FACED BY SMALL BUSINESS. (B) SOLVENCY GUIDELINES FOR INSURANCE COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to place the liability coverage issue in its proper context, 1 should like to return to the Question Period of November 4, 1985, when we, as Liberals, asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) to look very closely into the liability coverage crisis which was really exacerbating. His reply was to the effect that he was monitoring the situation very closely and that the Cabinet would adopt various measures.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the situation has greatly deteriorated now: institutions and small businesses have been receiving every day letters to the effect that when their insurance policies expire, there will be no renewals. Then, on January 16, as much as two months later, because the Conservative Government had failed to act on the pretext that it was a provincial jurisdiction, ten Liberal members asked for an


Adjournment Debate
investigation under the Combines Investigation Act to shed light on the whole business.
Then, Mr. Speaker, on January 20, I asked the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall)-following our request for an investigation the Government had finally started to move-what she was going to do to help small businesses, financial institutions, arenas, municipalities and others which had no liability coverage. The Minister replied that that very morning, she had met representatives of the insurance industry and that a Bill was forthcoming. Mr. Speaker, we are still waiting for it!
But in order to shed light on this problem, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read just a few of the great many letters which I have received so far, including one from a chartered accountants firm.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: INSURANCE-LIABILITY COVERAGE (A) DIFFICULTIES FACED BY SMALL BUSINESS. (B) SOLVENCY GUIDELINES FOR INSURANCE COMPANIES
speechtext: A C.G.A.?

subtopic: INSURANCE-LIABILITY COVERAGE (A) DIFFICULTIES FACED BY SMALL BUSINESS. (B) SOLVENCY GUIDELINES FOR INSURANCE COMPANIES
speechtext:
No, not a C.G.A., but a C.A. It is not mine, but the Montreal firm of Richler & Tabac which wrote:

I have read with interest and have seen on Canada AM (CTV) concerning the problem of liability insurance.
Our firm recently paid an increase of over 150 per cent when we had to renew our professional legal liability insurance. Not only that, but whereas in the past, there was a choice of insurers, we were obligated to deal with the only firm who was writing this type of policy in the Province of Quebec.
I do not know what is going on but I cannot believe that such increases can be tolerated when inflation has been limited to less than 5 per cent.
I hope that your efforts in requesting a federal investigation to this matter will be successful.
Another letter coming from Ontario reads:
Re: Product Liability Insurance
Our company, a wholly-owned Canadian corporation, is a manufacturer of machine tools and employs three hundred (300) people in Windsor, Ontario.
In the past 26 years no product liability claims have been registered against us, because quality and safety is essential and primary in the manufacture of our products.
On July 1, 1985, our product liability insurance increased in cost by eight (8) times with $100,000.00 deductible.
I could continue, but my time is limited. All industries, all sectors were affected. Canada Public Works has a problem with liability insurance. To conclude my remarks, I would like to quote:
The head of the Insurance Bureau of Canada says now is a good time to shake up the insurance system a little to see if there are any problems.
"I think the mechanisms that sell insurance, the mechanisms that underwrite risks have to be looked at," John Lyndon told CTV'S Question Period in an interview taped for broadcast Sunday.
Those are the words of John Lyndon, the head of the Insurance Bureau of Canada.
The funny part-or perhaps I should say the tragic part-of this whole crisis occurred to me when I read in a booklet
entitled Le Portefeuille d'assurances, at page 15, the following:

This is what has been predicted by Mr. Daniel Demers, an actuary for La Laurentienne Generate, at a luncheon of the Cercle d'Assurance Accidents de Montreal. He first indicated-
And I quote:
Recent social and legal events having created panic among insurers, reserves were increased to the point where a most profitable experience is predicted for 1985-86!
Mr. Speaker, people cannot get liability insurance, but companies are looking forward to a most profitable year. So we have every reason to ask the Government for action, and I know very well the point the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary will be making, that this again is a provincial responsibility. I am sorry, but the problems exists from Newfoundland to British Columbia, it is therefore a national problem. This Government should take the lead, get together with all provincial ministers in charge of insurance,and put an end to the crisis once and for all.

companies. That is what she said. But solvency is not the problem, the problem has to do with premiums and hat falls within provincial jurisdiction.
